title: The Second Law is general but not universally valid

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The Second Law is general but not universally valid

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is an important and general principle but is not universally valid; many systems in nature behave like rule 37R and do not show a uniform trend toward increasing randomness.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And indeed I strongly suspect that there are many systems in nature which behave in more or less the same way. The Second Law is an important and quite general principle—but it is not universally valid.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 9, “Fundamental Physics”; section “Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics” (from p. 441), p. 457. Scope: physical, biological and other natural systems to which the Second Law is applied

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch09-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.40

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Many thermodynamic datasets exist, but only restricted formulations can be tested cleanly. The broad analogy to rule 37R and universal scope make the claim underdetermined without substantial reinterpretation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify closed natural systems, coarse-graining, entropy measure, and observation interval, then search existing records for reproducible entropy decreases inconsistent with fluctuation theory. A confirmed violation under those definitions would refute universality; ordinary local ordering with compensating entropy export would not.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim conflates randomness with thermodynamic entropy.

Natural systems comparable to rule 37R are unspecified.

System boundaries and coarse-graining determine apparent violations.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Equilibrium thermodynamic tables and scattered small-system experiments can test pieces of the claim: macroscopic matter usually thermalizes, and short-time entropy decreases occur. They do not constitute a representative sample of natural systems evolving without a trend toward randomness. The universal-sounding qualification of the Second Law is only partly constrained.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Survey entropy-production time series for closed and isolated natural systems and test for a uniform trend toward randomness versus long-lived non-monotonic fluctuations. A large class of systems with no systematic trend would support the claim; a restriction of failures to brief microscopic fluctuations would support only a much weaker exception.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Microscopic fluctuation theorems already qualify the Second Law without systems behaving like rule 37R.

No public census samples natural systems widely enough to support or refute 'many'.
